steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a convergent version of iLQR for safe trajectory planning and control of legged robots. It should motivate agile motions like jumping, explain why they are hard to control, and introduce our method and what it improves.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: dynamic, agile legged motions and their risks
- Why they are hard: hybrid and underactuated trajectories
- Limits of the obvious fix (higher gains); our idea instead
- Contribution: convergent iLQR and its advantages

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Research in legged robotics has been focusing more and more on highly dynamic and agile motions like jumping, leaping, and landing. If these capabilities could be implemented reliably, legged robots would perform better in applications such as navigating extraterrestrial or urban environments, where the robot may need to jump up on ledges or leap across chasms. But jumping and leaping are dangerous maneuvers, and when they fail the outcome is often catastrophic for the robot.

These actions are challenging because the trajectories they induce are both hybrid and underactuated, and both of these make controlling legged robots harder. A system is hybrid if it undergoes discrete changes in state and/or dynamics, and it is underactuated if there is a direction of acceleration in state space that no valid input can command. Even if an underactuated system is controllable, getting it to a desired target state may take a lot of time and control effort, and neither of them may be readily available. For example, a robot jumping in the air can not choose arbitrarily how much time it has until its feet touch down on the ground. So the controller has to spend a lot of effort correcting tracking errors before touchdown, otherwise discontinuous, unbounded saltation effects can cause arbitrarily large divergence when the incoming errors are not mitigated enough, e.g. with grazing impacts. One possible solution to improve stability is to increase the control gains, but this has a big drawback, because it makes robustness worse when there are modelling errors and uncertainties. In this work we instead leverage nonlinearities in continuous and hybrid dynamics which make some trajectories easier to stabilize than others, even with equivalent feedback controllers.

- Contribution
  - adaptation of iLQR trajectory optimization, better closed-loop convergence under equivalent feedback controller (same LQR weights), Fig. 1
  - convergent iLQR (\chi -iLQR), simulation: 3 improvements over standard iLQR (tracking from initial perturbations, less feedback control effort, robustness to large initial errors)
  - 2 more strengths vs existing methods: analysis simple to compute vs sum-of-squares; captures local tracking performance of closed-loop trajectory -> directly predicts experimental results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Research in legged robotics has been focusing more and more on highly dynamic and agile motions like jumping, leaping, and landing. If these capabilities could be implemented reliably, legged robots would perform better in applications such as navigating extraterrestrial or urban environments, where the robot may need to jump up on ledges or leap across chasms. But jumping and leaping are dangerous maneuvers, and when they fail the outcome is often catastrophic for the robot.

These actions are challenging because the trajectories they induce are both hybrid and underactuated, and both of these make controlling legged robots harder. A system is hybrid if it undergoes discrete changes in state and/or dynamics, and it is underactuated if there is a direction of acceleration in state space that no valid input can command. Even if an underactuated system is controllable, getting it to a desired target state may take a lot of time and control effort, and neither of them may be readily available. For example, a robot jumping in the air can not choose arbitrarily how much time it has until its feet touch down on the ground. So the controller has to spend a lot of effort correcting tracking errors before touchdown, otherwise discontinuous, unbounded saltation effects can cause arbitrarily large divergence when the incoming errors are not mitigated enough, e.g. with grazing impacts. One possible solution to improve stability is to increase the control gains, but this has a big drawback, because it makes robustness worse when there are modelling errors and uncertainties. In this work we instead leverage nonlinearities in continuous and hybrid dynamics which make some trajectories easier to stabilize than others, even with equivalent feedback controllers.

In this paper we present a new adaptation of the iLQR trajectory optimization algorithm that improves closed-loop convergence under an equivalent feedback controller (i.e. the LQR controller weights are not changed), as shown in Fig. 1. Our simulation results show that this convergent iLQR (\chi -iLQR) gives three improvements at the same time over standard iLQR: better tracking performance from initial perturbations, less feedback control effort over the trajectory, and better robustness to large initial errors. Compared to existing methods, \chi -iLQR also has two more key strengths. First, it is based on an analysis that is simple to compute compared to methods like sum-of-squares. Also, \chi -iLQR captures the local tracking performance of a closed-loop trajectory, and this directly predicts experimental results.

steps.text:
Research in legged robotics has been focusing more and more on highly dynamic and agile motions like jumping, leaping, and landing [1,2,3,4]. If these capabilities could be implemented reliably, legged robots would perform better in applications such as navigating extraterrestrial or urban environments, where the robot may need to jump up on ledges or leap across chasms. But jumping and leaping are dangerous maneuvers, and when they fail the outcome is often catastrophic for the robot.

These actions are challenging because the trajectories they induce are both hybrid and underactuated, and both of these make controlling legged robots harder. A system is hybrid if it undergoes discrete changes in state and/or dynamics [5,6], and it is underactuated if there is a direction of acceleration in state space that no valid input can command [7]. Even if an underactuated system is controllable, getting it to a desired target state may take a lot of time and control effort, and neither of them may be readily available. For example, a robot jumping in the air can not choose arbitrarily how much time it has until its feet touch down on the ground. So the controller has to spend a lot of effort correcting tracking errors before touchdown, otherwise discontinuous, unbounded saltation effects [8] can cause arbitrarily large divergence when the incoming errors are not mitigated enough, e.g. with grazing impacts. One possible solution to improve stability is to increase the control gains, but this has a big drawback, because it makes robustness worse when there are modelling errors and uncertainties [9]. In this work we instead leverage nonlinearities in continuous and hybrid dynamics which make some trajectories easier to stabilize than others, even with equivalent feedback controllers.

In this paper we present a new adaptation of the iLQR trajectory optimization algorithm that improves closed-loop convergence under an equivalent feedback controller (i.e. the LQR controller weights are not changed), as shown in Fig. 1. Our simulation results show that this convergent iLQR (\chi -iLQR) gives three improvements at the same time over standard iLQR: better tracking performance from initial perturbations, less feedback control effort over the trajectory, and better robustness to large initial errors. Compared to existing methods, \chi -iLQR also has two more key strengths. First, it is based on an analysis that is simple to compute compared to methods like sum-of-squares. Also, \chi -iLQR captures the local tracking performance of a closed-loop trajectory, and this directly predicts experimental results.

References:
[1] A. M. Johnson and D. E. Koditschek, “Toward a vocabulary of legged leaping,” in IEEE Intl. Conference on Robotics and Automation , Karlsruhe, Germany, May 2013, pp. 2553–2560.
[2] H. Kolvenbach, E. Hampp, P. Barton et al. , “Towards jumping locomotion for quadruped robots on the moon,” IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems , 2019.
[3] C. Nguyen and Q. Nguyen, “Contact-timing and trajectory optimization for 3d jumping on quadruped robots,” IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems , 2022.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Legged robotics research has increasingly focused on enabling highly dynamic and agile motions such as jumping, leaping, and landing [1,2,3,4]. Implementing these capabilities reliably would improve the performance of legged robots in applications such as extraterrestrial or urban environment navigation, where jumping up on ledges or leaping across chasms may be necessary. However, jumping and leaping are dangerous maneuvers, and failure often results in catastrophic outcomes for the robot.

What makes these actions challenging is that they induce trajectories that are both hybrid and underactuated, which doubly contributes to the difficulty of controlling legged robots. Broadly, a system is hybrid if it undergoes discrete changes in state and/or dynamics [5,6], and it is underactuated if there exists a direction of acceleration in state space that can not be commanded by any valid input [7]. Even when an underactuated system is controllable, driving it to a desired target state may require significant time and control effort, neither of which may be readily available. For instance, a robot jumping in the air can not arbitrarily choose how much time it has until its feet touchdown on the ground. The controller therefore needs to spend a lot of effort correcting tracking errors prior to touchdown, or else discontinuous, unbounded saltation effects [8] can cause arbitrarily large divergence if incoming errors are not sufficiently mitigated, e.g. with grazing impacts. Increasing control gains is one possible way to improve stability, though it comes with the large drawback of worsening robustness to modelling errors and uncertainties [9]. Instead, this work leverages nonlinearities in continuous and hybrid dynamics that make some trajectories easier to stabilize than others, even under equivalent feedback controllers.

This paper presents a novel adaptation of the iLQR trajectory optimization algorithm that improves closed-loop convergence under an equivalent feedback controller (i.e. without changing the LQR controller weights), as shown in Fig. 1. Our simulation results show that this convergent iLQR (\chi -iLQR) achieves three simultaneous improvements over standard iLQR: better tracking performance from initial perturbations, reduced feedback control effort over the trajectory, and improved robustness to large initial errors. Compared to existing methods, \chi -iLQR has two additional key strengths. First, it is based on an analysis that is simple to compute compared to methods such as sum-of-squares. Second, \chi -iLQR captures the local tracking performance of a closed-loop trajectory, which directly predicts experimental results.

References:
[1] A. M. Johnson and D. E. Koditschek, “Toward a vocabulary of legged leaping,” in IEEE Intl. Conference on Robotics and Automation , Karlsruhe, Germany, May 2013, pp. 2553–2560.
[2] H. Kolvenbach, E. Hampp, P. Barton et al. , “Towards jumping locomotion for quadruped robots on the moon,” IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems , 2019.
[3] C. Nguyen and Q. Nguyen, “Contact-timing and trajectory optimization for 3d jumping on quadruped robots,” IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems , 2022.
[4] Z. Li, X. B. Peng, P. Abbeel et al. , “Robust and versatile bipedal jumping control through multi-task reinforcement learning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.09450 , 2023.
[5] A. van der Schaft and J. Schumacher, “Complementarity modeling of hybrid systems,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control , 1998.
[6] J. Lygeros, K. H. Johansson, S. Simic et al. , “Dynamical properties of hybrid automata,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control , 2003.
[7] R. Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics , 2022. [Online]. Available: http://underactuated.mit.edu
[8] N. J. Kong, J. J. Payne, J. Zhu, and A. M. Johnson, “Saltation matrices: The essential tool for linearizing hybrid dynamical systems,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.06862 , 2023.
[9] M. A. Haidekker, Linear Feedback Controls , M. A. Haidekker, Ed. Elsevier, 2020.
